question: Will the UK increase the qualifying period for settlement to 10 years before May 2026?
summary: There is strong official momentum toward a 10-year baseline for settlement under an earned settlement framework, suggesting a high-probability shift.
However, the consultation process, potential transitional arrangements, and possible exemptions introduce near-term uncertainty about universal implementation by May 2026.
Implementation is targeted to begin in spring 2026, which supports near-term effect but does not guarantee completion by May 2026.
Objections are valid and justify a modest downward adjustment from the ensemble aggregate while retaining a predominantly favorable view.

justification.critique_assessment: The objections realistically identify near-term risks (consultation response, transitional rules, political/legal delays) that could slow enactment, so they are valid.

forecasts.reference-class: Earned settlement policy reform in the UK immigration system, proposing a 10-year standard qualifying period for settlement with route-based exemptions.

sources.claim: The default qualifying period for settlement will be increased from the current 5 years to 10 years, with potential reductions based on contributions under a time-adjustment model and four pillars.

The House of Commons Library summarises the May 2025 immigration white paper proposals, including increasing the standard qualifying period for permanent residence from five to ten years, with some cases qualifying sooner depending on consultation-chosen criteria.
Long residence is defined as 10 years of continuous lawful residence; this supports the trend toward longer settlement thresholds.

The white paper proposes changing the standard qualifying period for indefinite leave to remain from five years to ten years, with an 'earned settlement' pathway that could allow some applicants to qualify earlier.

In May 2025 the government published a white paper proposing a ten-year settlement qualifying period (with potential faster routes); as of August 2025 no changes had been enacted and a formal consultation was expected.
The government proposes earned settlement with a default qualifying period increased from 5 to 10 years, with reductions for integration and contribution.
The Home Office announced a major reform including doubling the permanent settlement qualifying period to 10 years.
Parliament's Library summarises the plan to increase the baseline qualifying period to 10 years for many migrants, with fast tracks for high earners and other routes.
The Home Office opened a consultation on doubling the ILR qualifying period to 10 years.
Legal migration changes could increase or reduce the qualifying period based on factors; baseline 10 years with potential reductions and increases.

causal-factors.name: Official policy adoption under earned settlement framework
causal-factors.rationale: The 2025 White Paper and accompanying consultation explicitly propose a baseline 10-year qualifying period with a time-adjustment model, signaling a strong upward push on settlement thresholds for most migrants.

causal-factors.name: Planned implementation from April 2026
causal-factors.rationale: Government plans indicate changes to immigration rules are to begin in April 2026, which would place the 10-year baseline in effect for new ILR applications by April/May 2026.

causal-factors.name: Consultation outcome and timetable uncertainty
causal-factors.rationale: While the consultation closed in February 2026, there is no fixed timetable for enactment, creating risk that changes could be delayed beyond May 2026.

causal-factors.name: Existence of high-earnings exemptions / fast-track routes
causal-factors.rationale: Some groups may qualify earlier under fast-tracks, introducing nuance to the 10-year baseline but not reversing the overall shift toward longer qualifying periods for most migrants.

causal-factors.name: Earned settlement framework officially proposed with 10-year baseline
causal-factors.rationale: GOV.UK and Home Office materials publicly describe raising the default settlement qualifying period to 10 years under an earned settlement model, with four pillars and a time-adjustment mechanism for reductions (source: GOV.UK earned settlement statements; November 2025 update).

causal-factors.name: Implementation timeline slated to start in April 2026
causal-factors.rationale: The House of Commons Library briefing notes that changes to permanent residence rules are planned to begin in April 2026, signaling near-term enactment ahead of May 2026 (source: Commons Library CBP-10267, Feb 2026).

causal-factors.name: Potential transitional arrangements/exemptions under consultation
causal-factors.rationale: The consultation explicitly discusses transitional arrangements and pathway-specific exemptions that could delay or soften universal application of the 10-year baseline (source: GOV.UK Earned settlement page, Annex sections).

causal-factors.name: Public/political opposition and risk of delays
causal-factors.rationale: Media reporting and petitions highlight opposition and potential legal/policy challenges, which could slow or alter rollout and reduce near-term probability of a uniform 10-year baseline by May 2026 (sources: Guardian and FT coverage, Feb–Mar 2026).

causal-factors.name: Stricter eligibility conditions embedded in the plan (English language, income, character)
causal-factors.rationale: The earned settlement model includes higher English requirements (B2), a minimum income test, and stricter character/recourse conditions, reinforcing the direction toward longer residency before settlement (sources: GOV.UK earned settlement statements; November 2025 update; 8 January 2026 English standard changes).

causal-factors.name: Regulatory pathway enables changes without primary legislation
causal-factors.rationale: House of Commons Library notes that most settlement rule changes can be made by amending immigration rules rather than requiring an Act of Parliament, increasing the likelihood of near-term adoption (source: Commons Library briefing CBP-10267, Feb 2026).

causal-factors.name: Long Residence route integration into the 10-year baseline
causal-factors.rationale: Official materials frame long residence as being folded into the new baseline framework, signaling a path toward a 10-year threshold as a trend (source: GOV.UK earned settlement materials; long residence reference).

causal-factors.name: Official earned settlement rollout with 10-year baseline and time-adjustment
causal-factors.rationale: GOV.UK and Commons Library describe a 10-year baseline with reductions via a time-adjustment model, forming the core of the reform and signaling likely enactment.

causal-factors.name: Phased rollout timing indicating implementation from spring 2026
causal-factors.rationale: Public statements and briefing notes indicate a phased rollout starting around April 2026, increasing the odds that the change is in effect by May 2026.

causal-factors.name: Public/political opposition and concerns about impacts
causal-factors.rationale: IPPR analyses and Guardian reporting highlight substantial concerns and potential political pushback, which could delay or constrain the final form of the policy.

causal-factors.name: Uncertainty about retrospective applicability to those already in the UK
causal-factors.rationale: The government has not settled whether changes apply retrospectively, creating policy uncertainty that could slow near-term enactment.

causal-factors.name: Group-specific exceptions (e.g., high earners) could yield earlier paths for some cohorts
causal-factors.rationale: Provisions for faster routes for certain groups could raise the probability for those cohorts, though the baseline remains 10 years for most applicants.

synthesis: Official reforms point to a 10-year settlement baseline with an earned pathway and near-term rollout beginning in 2026, but consultation outcomes and transitional provisions create meaningful risk of delay. The final probability is calibrated slightly below the ensemble due to these near-term uncertainties, though the momentum remains strong.
